text:
A: Alright? Can you hear me okay? I'm Gary.
B: Yes. Hi. I am Jurgita.
A: Jurgita. Have I said that right? I don't want to get it wrong.
B: Yes, is right.
A: Lovely. Where are you based then?
B: Wakefield.
A: Oh, up north! I'm Bridgwater, Somerset. You'll have had the cold weather, I expect. How's your day going?
B: Is okay. I'm tired. I did three long days this week, in care home. Twelve hours each.
A: Twelve hours, three days on the trot? Blimey, that's proper graft. I used to do long shifts at a food depot, nights mostly, but I was sat on a forklift half the time, not running about after people.
B: My husband drives forklift. In warehouse, off M62.
A: No way! What's he on, counterbalance or a reach truck?
B: I don't know. Big one. He talks about it, I don't listen.
A: Ha! My ex-wife said exactly that. Nineteen years I did it. I was the one they'd send the new starters to, showing them round, the agency lads and all, I knew everybody's name. Then my back went, a disc, and sciatica all down my left leg, so I've been signed off two year now. I keep the licence card in my wallet though, daft really. Anyway, sorry, I'm going off on one.
B: No, is okay. Back is very bad. In care home also, we have moving and handling training, but still, all the girls have bad back. Lifting, bending, all day.
A: Oh, I bet. You must be careful. Do they look after you, the management?
B: Management? No. They change rota again without asking anyone. And they don't pay enough for what we do. Some girls, they sit in the office on phone, same money as me.
A: That's not right, that. There was always one on our shift, you know, disappeared for a fag every twenty minutes.
B: Yes, exactly. Always one.
A: Mind you, I'd give anything to be back moaning about the rota. I'm on benefits now, and there's a review coming up, and I'll be honest with you, it worries me. I'm trying to get to sixteen hours somewhere. Caretaker, something like that.
B: Sixteen hours is good. Not too much.
A: That's what I'm hoping. I do the food bank two mornings, sorting stock, so that keeps me out the house. We had a load of tinned peaches come in this week, about two hundred tins, no idea why.
B: Peaches. Okay.
A: Everybody's having peaches, my love. Do you cook much, after them long days?
B: Not after twelve hours. Then is Chinese or Domino's. Days off I cook, potatoes, soup, meat. And I buy Lithuanian sausage from shop on Kirkgate, they had good ones this week.
A: Lithuanian, is it? I thought I couldn't place the accent. Is it a spicy sausage? I'm not good with spicy.
B: No, not spicy. Smoked. Is nice with bread.
A: Oh, I'd have a go at that. I'm plain, me. Cottage pie on a Sunday, put it in tubs, label them, Monday to Thursday sorted. Fish and chips Friday.
B: Labels? On tubs?
A: Labels, date on, everything. I'm a bit sad like that.
B: Darius would like you. He eats everything in fridge, no labels, nothing.
A: Well, you tell him from me, he wants to get some labels. What time do you have your tea then, after a shift?
B: After shift, eight, nine o'clock. Then I watch Married at First Sight and go to bed.
A: Married at First Sight! Leanne, my daughter, she watches that, she was telling me about some bloke who—
